title: The last time everyone is in the room

lines.text: Thirty-four degrees on the plateau and the blinds are down on the south side. Nine people, a jug of water already going warm, and Gustave Eiffel, who flew in last night and flies out at seven.
lines.plain: It is 34 degrees outside. The blinds on the south side are closed. Nine people are in the room. There is a jug of water and it is already warm. Gustave Eiffel arrived last night. His flight home is at 19:00.

lines.text: The agenda went out on the fifth, with the Business Case, the Charter, the Handbook, the Work Plan, both the Transition and the Business Implementation Plans, and the four logs.
lines.plain: The agenda was sent on 5 July. Attached to it were the Business Case, the Project Charter, the Project Handbook, the Work Plan, the Transition Plan, the Business Implementation Plan and the four project logs.
ref: All Project Plans (particularly the Transition & Business Implementation Plans)

lines.text: I have the Minutes. I asked for them, so nobody has to look at the floor.
lines.plain: I will write the Minutes of this meeting. I asked to do it, so that nobody else has to volunteer.
g: Minutes of Meeting
the written record of what a meeting decided, who was there and who does what next
ref: Ensure someone is designated to take the Minutes of Meeting (MoM).

lines.text: Before anything. Thank you. From the Division, from the institution, and from me. I am told this is normally warmer. It is not going to be.
lines.plain: First, thank you. Thank you from the Lending Operations Division, from the institution, and from me. People tell me that this speech is usually warmer than mine. Mine will not be.
ref: The Project Owner (PO) will normally express the organisation's appreciation to the whole project team and key project stakeholders.

lines.text: Say it to the fourth floor as well. They ran the parallel in January and nobody has been up there since May.
lines.plain: Please say it to the fourth floor too. Those people ran the parallel test in January. Nobody has visited them since May.

lines.text: Monday. With names.
lines.plain: I will do it on Monday, and I will name people.

lines.text: Numbers, then. Final cost eight point nine six million against eight point four baselined. Six point seven per cent over. Effort three thousand three hundred and seven person-days against three thousand one hundred.
lines.plain: Now the numbers. The final cost was 8.96 million euro. The approved budget was 8.4 million euro. That is 6.7 per cent more. The effort was 3,307 person-days against a plan of 3,100.
g: person-day
one person working for one day; the unit used to size and price project effort
baseline
the approved version of scope, cost and schedule that all later results are measured against
ref: Present project statistics and data on performance and achievements.

lines.text: Nearly all of it is data migration, and data migration was mine. Say that before somebody says it kindly.
lines.plain: Almost all of the extra cost is data migration. Data migration was my responsibility. Please say that clearly, before someone says it in a gentle way.

lines.text: Go-live on the fifteenth of May, which is the date in the Charter from March 2026. Scope: eleven changes approved, two postponed, one rejected. None of them touched the Business Case.
lines.plain: The system went live on 15 May 2028. That is the date written in the Project Charter, approved in March 2026. On scope: 11 changes were approved, 2 were postponed and 1 was rejected. None of them changed the Business Case.

lines.text: Quality. Compliance against the Quality Management Plan, all four reviews, and I have no reservation anywhere in it. Enjoy that. I do not say it often and I will not say it twice today.
lines.plain: Now quality. I checked the work against the Quality Management Plan across all four reviews. I have no objection anywhere. Enjoy that sentence. I do not say it often, and I will not say it again today.
ref: Project Quality Assurance (PQA) Should attend.

lines.text: SC5. I was told autumn.
lines.plain: Now SC5, the success criterion about the audit findings. I was told the answer would come in the autumn.
g: internal-audit finding
a written weakness raised by the institution's own auditors, closed only with evidence

lines.text: The closure letter came on the fourth. Both findings shut. Segregation of duties, and the audit trail. They had the evidence pack since May and it held.
lines.plain: Internal Audit sent the closure letter on 4 July 2028. Both findings are now closed: the one about who may do which step, and the one about the record of changes. The auditors had our evidence since May and it was good enough.

lines.text: While we are on the five. Who measures them after this month?
lines.plain: While we are talking about the five success criteria. Who measures them after July?

lines.text: Item nine.
lines.plain: That is item nine on the agenda.

lines.text: It is always item nine.
lines.plain: The difficult things are always at the end of the agenda.

lines.text: Contractor performance. Gustave is sitting in the room. I assume that was decided and not overlooked.
lines.plain: Now the contractor's performance. Gustave Eiffel is in the room. I assume someone decided that, and did not simply forget.

lines.text: Decided. We evaluate the contractor with the contractor here, or what we write down is gossip.
lines.plain: It was decided. We assess the contractor while the contractor is present. If we do it without him, what we write is only rumour.
ref: Also in this meeting team and contractor performance are evaluated, and ideas and recommendations for post-project work are discussed.

lines.text: Both releases on their baselined dates. The second one after they lost their lead architect and we lost ours. The configuration engine is better than the tender described. The migration estimate was optimistic and both signatures on it are in this room.
lines.plain: Levallois delivered both releases on the planned dates. They delivered the second one after they had lost their lead architect and we had lost ours. The product configuration engine is better than the tender promised. The estimate for data migration was too optimistic. Both people who signed that estimate are in this room.

lines.text: Harder than that. We priced a migration off a data model we had never been shown. It is in our own closing note. Whoever writes our next bid will read it. Put the evaluation in today's Minutes, please — it is the only thing I take home.
lines.plain: I will say it more strongly. We priced the data migration without ever seeing the data model. That sentence is in our own closing note. The person who writes our next offer will read it. Please put the evaluation in today's Minutes. It is the only thing I take home with me.

lines.text: Marie. Does it work?
lines.plain: Marie, does the system work?

lines.text: Ask me in January. I have had it eight weeks and it has not seen a December.
lines.plain: Ask me again in January. I have used it for eight weeks. It has not yet been through a December, which is our busiest time.

lines.text: Forty administrators retrained by the thirtieth of April. Two roles redesigned. Segregation of duties is in the platform now, not in Marie standing behind somebody at half past four.
lines.plain: 40 loan administrators were retrained by 30 April 2028. Two jobs were redesigned. The rule about who may do which step is now enforced by the system. Before, Marie Curie enforced it by standing behind a colleague at 16:30.

lines.text: Then the part I have to live with. I can tell the Board of Directors that it runs. I cannot tell them what it was worth. Not one of the five survives a second question.
lines.plain: Now the part I must accept. I can tell the Board of Directors that the system is running. I cannot tell them what it is worth. If anyone asks a second question about the five success criteria, I have no answer.

lines.text: Longer than this meeting. Give me until the seventeenth and I will bring you the section.
lines.plain: That takes longer than this meeting has. Give me until 17 July and I will bring you that part of the report.
ref: After the Project-End Review Meeting: 1. Compile Lessons Learned and Post-Project Recommendations. 2. Produce the Project-End Report.

lines.text: Florence's assistant puts her head round the door at eleven ten. The Board of Directors preparation has moved to two. The Lessons Learned session is at half past one.
lines.plain: At 11:10 Florence Nightingale's assistant opens the door. The Board of Directors preparation has been moved to 14:00. The Lessons Learned session starts at 13:30.
g: Lessons Learned
written notes on what worked and what did not, kept so that other projects can reuse them

lines.text: Grace can hold the business side this afternoon. Do I have to sit and listen to people say what they would have done differently?
lines.plain: Grace Hopper can represent the business side this afternoon. Do I have to sit and listen to people saying what they would have done differently?
ref: Business Manager (BM) Represents the business side and the stakeholders.

choice.prompt: Florence is asking to be let out of the afternoon. What do you do?
choice.promptPlain: Florence Nightingale wants to skip the afternoon session. What do you do?

options.t: Tell her plainly that her attendance is required, and that the Steering Committee collects the lessons this afternoon.
options.tPlain: Tell her clearly that the Project Owner must attend, and that the Steering Committee gathers the lessons this afternoon.

reply.text: Then I move the Board preparation and I sit through all of it. But say it that way. If it is required, tell me it is required. Do not ask me as though it were a favour.
reply.plain: Then I will move the Board preparation and stay for the whole session. But say it like that. If it is required, tell me it is required. Do not ask me as if I were doing you a favour.

options.why: Guide p.64 lists the Project Owner's attendance as required, in its own row, next to the Project Core Team's. The PO is also the person who expresses the organisation's appreciation. Guide p.65 adds that the Project Steering Committee should be invited to the Lessons Learned session so its members can carry the lessons to other projects — and Florence chairs the PSC. The PSC is Accountable for the meeting and the PM is Responsible for organising it, which includes making attendance real rather than nominal.
options.whyPlain: Page 64 says the Project Owner must attend. It is a separate line in the table, next to the Project Core Team. Page 65 says the Steering Committee should be invited to the Lessons Learned session, so its members can take the lessons to other projects. Florence chairs that committee. The committee is accountable for the meeting; you are responsible for organising it. Organising it includes making sure the required people are actually there.
ref: Project Owner (PO) Attendance is required.

options.t: Let Grace stand in. The Business Manager represents the business side and the stakeholders anyway.
options.tPlain: Let Grace Hopper replace her. The Business Manager represents the business side and the stakeholders anyway.

reply.text: I represent the business side. I do not represent her. If somebody asks me this afternoon whether the Division will own benefit tracking, I cannot answer, and you know I cannot.
reply.plain: I represent the business side. I do not represent Florence. If someone asks me this afternoon whether the Division will own the benefit measurement, I cannot answer. You know that I cannot.

options.why: The guide gives the BM and the PO separate rows for a reason: the BM represents the business side and the stakeholders, while the PO's attendance is required in its own right (p.64). The PO is only Consulted on this activity, but becomes Accountable a fortnight later at Administrative Closure (p.67) — so a person who was not in the room is being asked to approve what came out of it.
options.whyPlain: Page 64 lists the Business Manager and the Project Owner separately. The Business Manager speaks for the business side. The Project Owner must be there in person. Today the Project Owner is only consulted. But two weeks later, at Administrative Closure, she is the one who is accountable and signs (page 67). She would then be approving a result she did not see.
ref: Business Manager (BM) Represents the business side and the stakeholders.

options.t: Split it. Close the meeting now, and hold a short session with the Project Owner alone next week.
options.tPlain: Divide it. End the meeting now and hold a short separate session with the Project Owner next week.

reply.text: Then we have the same conversation twice and end with two versions of it. Half these people are on other projects by Wednesday.
reply.plain: Then we hold the same discussion twice and we end with two different versions of it. By Wednesday half of these people are working on other projects.

options.why: Guide p.65 states that the Lessons Learned session should be part of the Project-End Review Meeting; separate sessions belong at the end of phases or at major milestones, not after the project has ended. Splitting it produces a team debrief and a management debrief that never meet, which is exactly the loss the note on that page warns about.
options.whyPlain: Page 65 says the Lessons Learned session should be part of this meeting. Separate sessions are for the end of a phase or a big milestone, not for after the project is over. If you split it, you get one discussion for the team and another for management, and they never meet.
ref: The Lessons Learned session should be a part of the Project-End Review Meeting (though separate sessions could be organised at the end of project phases or major milestones).

options.t: Excuse her. The appreciation is on the record and the rest is detail the Project Manager writes up afterwards.
options.tPlain: Let her go. Her thanks are recorded, and you can write up the rest afterwards.

reply.text: Then twelve subjects of the Project-End Report get written by one person who was in the room, for an approver who was not. I still have to review it, and I will write that down.
reply.plain: Then one person who was in the room writes all twelve subjects of the Project-End Report, for an approver who was not in the room. I must still review that report, and I will record this.

options.why: The Project-End Report is produced after this meeting and takes the meeting's Minutes as its main input (p.66), so leaving the PO out makes the report the record of a single perspective. The participant list on p.64 is not a courtesy list: the PO's attendance is required, the PCT's is required, PQA should attend, and contributions from other roles may be valuable.
options.whyPlain: The Project-End Report is written after this meeting, and its main input is the Minutes of this meeting (page 66). If the Project Owner is not here, the report records only one point of view. The list of participants on page 64 is not a polite invitation list. It says who must attend and who should attend.
ref: Inputs • Project-End Review Meeting Minutes (MoM)

you.o: Responsible for organising this meeting, and for writing the Project-End Report that follows it.
you.k: Knows the final figures, and that no success criterion can be signed off today.
you.w: Wants the contractor evaluated on the record, with the contractor in the room.
you.f: Afraid the Project Owner leaves before the lessons are collected.

nightingale.o: Project Owner. Accountable for the benefits, but only Consulted on today's meeting.
nightingale.k: Knows the platform is live, that SC5 closed on 4 July, and that 2029 holds the rest.
nightingale.w: Wants the thanks said once, and to reach the Board preparation this afternoon.
nightingale.f: Afraid the business case is judged before a single benefit number exists.

leonardo.o: Solution Provider. Accountable for the delivered platform, including the data migration overrun.
leonardo.k: Knows the overrun is almost entirely his, and that he has no lead architect left.
leonardo.w: Wants the overrun put on the estimate rather than on his people.
leonardo.f: Afraid the contractor evaluation becomes a verdict on individuals who have gone.

hopper.o: Business Manager. Ran the retraining, and from August runs the live operation.
hopper.k: Knows 40 administrators are trained and that nobody has yet named a benefits owner.
hopper.w: Wants to hear today who measures SC1 to SC5 after July.
hopper.f: Afraid the measurement lands on her with no time, no data and no mandate.

curie.o: User Representative. Accepted the deliverables, and now uses them every morning.
curie.k: Knows the platform has run eight weeks, with no December and no crisis in them.
curie.w: Wants the fourth floor thanked, and no verdict on the system yet.
curie.f: Afraid a quiet July is turned into a claim about a whole year.

deming.o: Project Quality Assurance, independent of the Project Manager. Should attend this meeting.
deming.k: Knows compliance against the Quality Management Plan is clean for the first time.
deming.w: Wants the meeting to produce evidence rather than warmth.
deming.f: Afraid the closing documents are written to please instead of to record.

lovelace.o: Business Analyst in the Project Core Team. Designated to take today's Minutes.
lovelace.k: Knows the Lessons Learned register holds forty-one entries, and which of them are soft.
lovelace.w: Wants the room's exact words written down, including the uncomfortable ones.
lovelace.f: Afraid she goes back to the fourth floor on Monday with things left unsaid.

eiffel.o: Contractor's Project Manager. Answerable to Levallois for closing the contract cleanly.
eiffel.k: Knows both releases landed on date, and that the migration bid was wrong.
eiffel.w: Wants the evaluation in today's Minutes, before his contract ends on 31 July.
eiffel.f: Afraid the record is written after he leaves, where he cannot answer it.

note: Guide check: the Closing Phase starts with the Project-End Review Meeting (p.63). RASCI on p.64 is AGB=I, PSC=A, PO=C, BM=S, BIG=C, SP=C, PM=R, PCT=C — the Project Steering Committee is Accountable, the Project Manager is Responsible for organising it. Attendance is not uniform and the guide is precise: the Project Owner's attendance is required, the Project Core Team's attendance is required, Project Quality Assurance should attend, and the Business Manager represents the business side and the stakeholders. During the meeting the PO normally expresses the organisation's appreciation, someone is designated to take the Minutes, project statistics and performance are presented, and team and contractor performance are evaluated. Afterwards there are exactly three steps: compile Lessons Learned and Post-Project Recommendations, produce the Project-End Report, communicate the results to the relevant stakeholders. Approver: the PSC. Note the trap — the PO is only Consulted here. The PO's moment of accountability is Administrative Closure. Page 64.
notePlain: Rule: the Closing Phase opens with the Project-End Review Meeting (page 63). RASCI row on page 64: AGB=I, PSC=A, PO=C, BM=S, BIG=C, SP=C, PM=R, PCT=C. So the Project Steering Committee is accountable and approves; you, the Project Manager, are responsible for organising the meeting. Who comes is not the same for everyone. The Project Owner must attend. The Project Core Team must attend. Project Quality Assurance should attend. The Business Manager speaks for the business side and the stakeholders. In the meeting the Project Owner thanks the team, someone is named to write the Minutes, the numbers are presented, and the team and the contractor are assessed. After the meeting there are three steps: collect the lessons and the post-project recommendations, write the Project-End Report, and tell the stakeholders the result. Trap to remember: today the Project Owner is only consulted. Her moment to approve comes later, at Administrative Closure. Page 64.

title: Give me the pen

lines.text: Half past one. The sandwiches were a mistake. Somebody opened the blinds for a photograph nobody had asked for and the room is at twenty-eight degrees. Albert Einstein has come down from the Architecture Office for the afternoon.
lines.plain: It is 13:30. The sandwiches were a bad idea. Someone opened the blinds for a photograph that nobody wanted, and the room is now at 28 degrees. Albert Einstein has come down from the Architecture Office for the afternoon.

lines.text: One honest question before we start, and I am not being difficult.
lines.plain: I have one honest question before we start. I am not trying to cause trouble.

lines.text: Nobody has perspective eight weeks after a go-live. September. You would get considered answers instead of tired ones.
lines.plain: Nobody can judge a project clearly eight weeks after it goes live. Do this in September. Then you get careful answers instead of tired ones.
ref: The Lessons Learned session should be a part of the Project-End Review Meeting (though separate sessions could be organised at the end of project phases or major milestones).

lines.text: Who is in the room in September?
lines.plain: Who will still be here in September?

lines.text: Not me. Fourth floor from Monday, with a queue of my own.
lines.plain: Not me. From Monday I am back on the fourth floor with my own work waiting.

lines.text: Not me. My contract ends on the thirty-first and I am on a plane at seven tonight.
lines.plain: Not me. My contract ends on 31 July and my flight leaves at 19:00 tonight.
g: framework contract
a standing agreement with a supplier; individual orders, called call-offs, are placed under it

lines.text: Two of your testers go the same day.
lines.plain: Two of the contractor's test engineers leave on the same day.

lines.text: I still think September gives better answers. I accept that it gives them to nobody.
lines.plain: I still believe September would give better answers. But I accept that in September there would be nobody left to give them.

lines.text: We have the register in any case. Forty-one entries since Planning, each written the week the thing happened.
lines.plain: We have the register anyway. It holds 41 entries made since the Planning Phase. Each one was written in the same week as the event it describes.
g: Lessons Learned register
the running list a project keeps of what it learned, written while the project is still going
ref: Note: Improvement opportunities and Post-Project Recommendations should be captured in some form as they come up during the project.

lines.text: Then read it out and let everybody go home.
lines.plain: Then read the register out loud and let everyone leave.

lines.text: The register is what people wrote on their own. It is not what they say to each other.
lines.plain: The register holds what each person wrote alone. That is not the same as what people say when they are together.
ref: When project team members share their perspectives and provide feedback it provides useful insights

lines.text: It really is not. Entry nineteen says migration rehearsal effort underestimated. It does not say that Nikola told me in November and I assumed he was managing it himself.
lines.plain: That is true. Entry 19 says the effort for the migration rehearsal was estimated too low. It does not say that Nikola Tesla told me about it in November, and that I assumed he was handling it himself.

lines.text: He was not managing it. He was rewriting it.
lines.plain: He was not handling it. He was rewriting it.

lines.text: Which is a lesson, and it has just been captured, and it is twenty to two.
lines.plain: That is a lesson. It has just been recorded. The time is 13:40.

lines.text: I am here because the Steering Committee was invited. I will take two of these into the target architecture review in October. That is not manners. It is the only road they travel on.
lines.plain: I am here because the Steering Committee was invited. I will take two of these lessons into the architecture review in October. I am not being polite. That review is the only way these lessons reach other projects.
ref: The Project Steering Committee (PSC) should be invited to the Lessons Learned session(s) as this will allow its members to transfer the Lessons Learned to other projects.

lines.text: Explain that to me properly. Why is a Steering Committee sitting in a room about what went wrong?
lines.plain: Explain that properly to me. Why does a Steering Committee sit in a meeting about mistakes?

lines.text: Because a lesson that stays inside the project it came from is a memory. The four of you sit on six other projects between you.
lines.plain: Because a lesson that never leaves its own project is only a memory. The four members of this committee sit on six other projects in total.
ref: To avoid making the same mistakes twice, Lessons Learned should be shared with other project managers.

lines.text: There is a second guideline on that page and nobody has said it out loud.
lines.plain: There is a second guideline on that page of the guide, and nobody has said it aloud yet.

lines.text: Say it.
lines.plain: Please say it.

lines.text: The person running this session should not be the person the session is about.
lines.plain: The person who leads this session should not be the person the session is about.
ref: It may be preferable to have the Lessons Learned session facilitated by someone who has not been intimately involved in the project, allowing the Project Manager (PM) to contribute as a participant.

lines.text: Meaning me.
lines.plain: You mean me.

lines.text: Twenty-six months of this belong to the Project Manager. If you hold the pen, half the room is kind to you and the other half aims. Give me the pen and answer when you are asked.
lines.plain: Twenty-six months of this project belong to the Project Manager. If you lead the session, half the room will be gentle with you and the other half will attack you. Give me the pen. Then take part, and answer when someone asks you a question.

lines.text: I would pay to watch that.
lines.plain: I would like to see that.

lines.text: I moved a Board preparation for this. Decide.
lines.plain: I moved a Board preparation meeting so that I could be here. Make a decision.
g: Post-Project Recommendations
proposed work after the project ends: fixes, extensions, follow-up projects, and benefit checks

choice.prompt: How do you run the Lessons Learned session?
choice.promptPlain: How do you run the Lessons Learned session?

options.t: Run it now, inside this meeting, with Deming holding the pen so you can take part as a participant.
options.tPlain: Hold it now, inside this meeting. Ask Deming to lead it, so that you can take part like everyone else.

reply.text: Then I take the pen. Six headings, twenty minutes each, and the Project Manager sits down and answers when asked, like everybody else in the room.
reply.plain: Then I will lead it. Six headings, twenty minutes for each one. The Project Manager sits down and answers questions like everyone else.

options.why: Guide p.65 gives both guidelines this option follows: the Lessons Learned session should be part of the Project-End Review Meeting, and it may be preferable to have it facilitated by someone not intimately involved in the project, allowing the Project Manager to contribute as a participant. The RASCI is unchanged from the meeting itself — PSC=A, PM=R — so you remain Responsible for the session happening, not for chairing it.
options.whyPlain: Page 65 gives two guidelines and this option follows both. First, the Lessons Learned session should be part of the Project-End Review Meeting. Second, it is often better if someone outside the project leads it, so the Project Manager can join in as a participant. The RASCI row does not change: the Steering Committee is accountable, you are responsible. You are responsible for the session happening. You are not required to chair it.
ref: It may be preferable to have the Lessons Learned session facilitated by someone who has not been intimately involved in the project, allowing the Project Manager (PM) to contribute as a participant.

options.t: Hold a separate session in September, when people have distance from the go-live and can think properly.
options.tPlain: Hold a separate session in September, when people have had time to think about the go-live.

reply.text: In September I am not an employee of Levallois. Everything I know about how you and I estimated that migration gets on a plane with me tonight.
reply.plain: In September I no longer work for Levallois. Everything I know about how we estimated the data migration leaves with me tonight.

options.why: Separate Lessons Learned sessions are allowed at the end of project phases or at major milestones (p.65), which is not the same as after closure. The note on the same page is the point: in longer projects the ideas get lost by the time the Closing Phase arrives — and here the Core Team, the contractor and the business analyst all disperse within three weeks.
options.whyPlain: Page 65 allows separate sessions at the end of a phase or at a big milestone. It does not allow them after the project is closed. The note on the same page explains why: in long projects the ideas are lost by the time Closing arrives. Here the Core Team, the contractor and the business analyst all leave within three weeks.
ref: Otherwise, particularly in longer projects, the ideas might get lost by the time the project reaches the Closing Phase.

options.t: Publish the running register. Forty-one entries captured as they arose is exactly what the guide asks for.
options.tPlain: Publish the running register instead. It already holds 41 entries, written as things happened.

reply.text: Then entry nineteen stands as it is and nobody ever learns that I sat on it for a month. The register is the evidence. It is not the conversation.
reply.plain: Then entry 19 stays as it is, and nobody learns that I kept the information to myself for a month. The register is the evidence. It is not the discussion.

options.why: Capturing improvement opportunities and recommendations as they come up is a note on p.65 that protects against loss; it does not replace the session, which is the first guideline on that page. The session exists so that team members share perspectives and hear each other, which is what produces the insight the requestor side uses to manage post-project activities.
options.whyPlain: Writing lessons down as they happen is a note on page 65. It protects you against losing them. It does not replace the session, which is the first guideline on that page. The session exists so that people share their views and hear each other. That is what produces the insight the business side needs after the project.
ref: The purpose of formal Lessons Learned and Post-Project Recommendations is to make it possible for project teams and the permanent organisation at large to benefit from the experience acquired during the project.

options.t: Send a structured questionnaire to the wider group instead, and compile the answers into the report.
options.tPlain: Send a written questionnaire to a wider group instead, and put the answers in the report.

reply.text: I answered a questionnaire in March. I ticked four boxes and wrote the word fine. Ask me in this room and I will tell you what I told you on the twenty-seventh of April.
reply.plain: I answered a questionnaire in March. I ticked four boxes and wrote the word fine. Ask me here, in this room, and I will tell you exactly what I told you on 27 April.

options.why: The guide does recommend structured questionnaires or interviews, but for collecting lessons from a broader group of stakeholders (p.65) — as a supplement to the session, not a substitute for it. Replacing the session with a form loses the structured discussion across phases and categories that the same page requires, and loses everything that only surfaces when two people disagree.
options.whyPlain: Page 65 does recommend questionnaires and interviews, but for collecting lessons from a wider group of stakeholders. They are an addition to the session, not a replacement. A form cannot give you the structured discussion across phases and categories that the same page requires. It also loses everything that only appears when two people disagree in a room.
ref: Use a structured approach to collecting lessons learned from a broader group of stakeholders via questionnaires, or structured interviews.

you.o: Responsible for organising the gathering of Lessons Learned; still Responsible even if you do not chair it.
you.k: Knows the register is complete and that the room disperses within three weeks.
you.w: Wants the session held today, before the people who lived it scatter.
you.f: Afraid that chairing it himself would quietly edit the worst entries.

nightingale.o: Project Owner, and chair of the Project Steering Committee that was invited to this session.
nightingale.k: Knows she moved a Board preparation, and does not yet know why lessons travel upward.
nightingale.w: Wants a reason to be here that is better than attendance.
nightingale.f: Afraid the afternoon is a ritual with no product at the end of it.

leonardo.o: Solution Provider. Contributes his own and his division's experience of the project.
leonardo.k: Knows perspective improves with time, and now knows nobody will be left to have it.
leonardo.w: Wanted September; wants, failing that, an accurate record of the migration.
leonardo.f: Afraid tired answers become the permanent version of what happened.

hopper.o: Business Manager. Represents the requestor's point of view in the session.
hopper.k: Knows the register by heart because the Business Implementation Group filled half of it.
hopper.w: Wants the business lessons kept separate from the technical ones.
hopper.f: Afraid the day ends without anyone naming who owns the benefits.

curie.o: User Representative. Contributes the acceptance and daily-use experience.

notePlain: Rule: the Lessons Learned activity has the same RASCI row as the meeting around it. Page 65 prints AGB=I, PSC=A, PO=C, BM=S, BIG=C, SP=C, PM=R, PCT=C. lines.plain: The clause worked. Our platform architect resigned in April 2027. You received a named replacement and three weeks of handover, because the contract required it, and because you paid for that sentence in 2026.

A project kept open to watch its own benefits is really an operation, but it still carries a project's governance and cost. note: Guide check: §3.2.6 (p.17) names three PM² phase gates and only three — RfP at the end of Initiating, RfE at the end of Planning, RfC at the end of Executing. There is no gate at the end of the Closing Phase. The Closing Phase instead starts with the Project-End Review Meeting and ends with the Project Owner's final approval, which marks administrative closure (p.63). A Closing sheet of the Phase-Exit Review Checklist still exists, but the glossary (p.131) describes these checklists as documents used by the Project Manager to ensure all necessary items are in place before the project proceeds or is closed: a self-assessment supporting the PO's decision, not an approval and not a gate. On the report itself, p.66 gives AGB=I, PSC=A, PO=C, BM=S, BIG=C, SP=C, PM=R, PCT=C, requires the twelve mandated subjects, and requires the document to be placed in a central project repository or knowledge database for use by future projects. notePlain: Rule: PM² has three phase gates and only three (page 17). Ready for Planning at the end of Initiating. Ready for Executing at the end of Planning. Ready for Closing at the end of Executing. There is no gate at the end of Closing. Instead, the Closing Phase begins with the Project-End Review Meeting and ends with the Project Owner's final approval (page 63). There is still a Closing sheet in the Phase-Exit Review Checklist. The glossary on page 131 explains what it is for: the Project Manager uses it to check that everything is in place before the project moves on or is closed. It supports the Project Owner's decision. It is not an approval and it is not a gate. For the report itself, page 66 gives the row AGB=I, PSC=A, PO=C, BM=S, BIG=C, SP=C, PM=R, PCT=C, lists the twelve required subjects, and requires the report to be stored in a central repository for future projects. note: Guide check: Administrative Closure is the exception in chapter 8. RASCI on p.67 is AGB=I, PSC=C, PO=A, BM=C, BIG=I, SP=C, PM=R, PCT=I, so the Project Owner is Accountable and gives final approval, while the PSC — Accountable for the three preceding activities — drops to Consulted. The five steps are: review, organise and archive all documentation and records; release all resources; ensure the project is approved and accepted by the stakeholders; ensure the PO gives final project approval and closes the project; and verify that all contractual obligations have been fulfilled. The Project Support Office assists with reviewing, organising and archiving. The outputs are the updated Projects Archive and the Project Acceptance Note if required. The Project Team is officially dissolved and all resources are released, and formal closure brings project mode to an end and allows operations mode to commence. A contractor warranty running past closure is not an open project — it is a contract obligation held by operations. Approver: the PO. Page 67.
notePlain: Rule: Administrative Closure is the exception in chapter 8. The row on page 67 is AGB=I, PSC=C, PO=A, BM=C, BIG=I, SP=C, PM=R, PCT=I. The Project Owner is accountable and gives the final approval. The Steering Committee, which was accountable for the three earlier activities, is only consulted here. There are five steps. Review, organise and archive all documents and records. Release all the people. Make sure the stakeholders approve and accept the project. Make sure the Project Owner gives final approval and closes the project. Check that all contract obligations are met. The Project Support Office helps with the archiving. The outputs are the updated Projects Archive and, if required, the Project Acceptance Note. The team is formally dissolved and everyone is released. Formal closure ends project mode and starts operations mode. A supplier warranty that lasts beyond closure is not an open project. It is a contract, and operations holds it. Approver: the Project Owner. Page 67.

title: Value date Monday
where: ESM, Kirchberg — Lending Operations, fourth floor

lines.text: Rain over the Kirchberg plateau, the kind that hangs rather than falls. Not light yet. The fourth floor has been switched on since half past six.
lines.plain: It is raining over Kirchberg. The rain hangs in the air rather than falling. It is still dark. The lights on the fourth floor have been on since 06:30.

lines.text: You are not here for CASTOR. There is a Project Initiation Request in your bag for something else entirely, dated Monday, and you have read it once. Grace Hopper has a chair pulled out already.
lines.plain: You are not here for Project CASTOR. In your bag there is a Project Initiation Request for a completely different project. It is dated Monday and you have read it once. Grace Hopper has already pulled out a chair for you.
g: Project Initiation Request
the one-page document that asks permission to explore a problem and write a Business Case

lines.text: Twenty minutes, then I have a rollover to prepare and you have a different problem to go and have.
lines.plain: We have twenty minutes. After that I must prepare a bond rollover, and you must go and start a different problem.

lines.text: Third and fourth quarter of 2028, out of the Division's operational report and nothing of yours. SC1: one working day, forty-one disbursements, two of them on the thirty-first of December. SC2: same-day reconciliation, every day, including the week of the November rollover. SC4: zero re-keyed fields, from fourteen hundred a quarter.
lines.plain: These are the figures for the third and fourth quarters of 2028. They come from the Division's own operational report, not from any project document. SC1: one working day, measured over 41 payments, two of them on 31 December. SC2: reconciliation on the same day, every day, including the week of the November rollover. SC4: no fields typed again by hand, down from about 1,400 every three months.

lines.text: SC5 stays closed unless Internal Audit reopens it. SC3 is still a blank line, because there is still no new instrument to onboard. And the full-year statement for 2029 goes to the Corporate Investment Board in February 2030, which is nineteen months after your cost centre closed.
lines.plain: SC5 stays closed unless Internal Audit opens it again. SC3 is still empty, because there is still no new lending product to set up. The statement for the whole of 2029 goes to the Corporate Investment Board in February 2030. That is nineteen months after your project's cost centre closed.
ref: Note that project outcomes and benefits are often realised only after the project has closed.

lines.text: And it has not been your file since the twenty-eighth of July. That is not a complaint. It is the arrangement, and it was the right one.
lines.plain: And it has not been your file since 28 July 2028. That is not a complaint. It is the agreement we made, and it was the right one.

lines.text: Henry Gantt comes off the lift with a laptop under one arm and the particular walk of somebody who has just found who he was looking for.
lines.plain: Henry Gantt comes out of the lift with a laptop under one arm. He walks like a man who has just found the person he was looking for.

lines.text: The backstop onboarding project has had a project manager since the seventh. She pulled the CASTOR Project-End Report out of the archive on her second day, and she has a question I cannot answer.
lines.plain: The backstop onboarding project has had a project manager since 7 January. On her second day she took the CASTOR Project-End Report out of the archive. She has a question that I cannot answer.

lines.text: She wants to know what it cost you to postpone CR-014, and whether she can simply re-open it.
lines.plain: She wants to know what it cost you to postpone change request CR-014, and whether she can simply re-open it.

lines.text: Section 3.3 for why it happened, section 7 for what we learned from it, the Change Log for the money. A hundred and forty-five person-days and three hundred and ninety-two thousand at 2027 prices, against a data model that has changed twice since. Tell her to re-estimate, not to re-open.
lines.plain: Section 3.3 explains why it happened. Section 7 gives what we learned. The Change Log has the money: 145 person-days and 392,000 euro at 2027 prices. The data model has changed twice since then. Tell her to make a new estimate, not to re-open the old one.

lines.text: So that is what the report was for.
lines.plain: So that is the purpose of the report.

lines.text: It is the only thing it was ever for. Nobody writes one for the people who were in the room.
lines.plain: That is the only purpose it ever had. Nobody writes a Project-End Report for the people who were in the room.
ref: This document should be part of a central project repository or knowledge database describing project experiences, best practices and common pitfalls.

lines.text: Project Support Office. You will have heard that I am a Project Owner again. Same division, smaller project, and this time I read chapter eight before we started rather than after.
lines.plain: Good morning, Project Support Office. You will have heard that I am a Project Owner again. It is the same division and a smaller project. This time I read chapter 8 of the guide before we started, not afterwards.

lines.text: In July I told you that a report which cannot state its benefits is a report admitting failure. I was wrong, and I have had six months to be wrong in. I do not intend to say it twice, so you will have to remember it for me.
lines.plain: In July I told you that a report which cannot state its benefits is a report admitting failure. I was wrong, and I have had six months to think about it. I do not intend to say this a second time, so you will have to remember it for me.

lines.text: She asked for twenty minutes on how it goes. Not the artefacts. She has the artefacts, they are all in the archive. How it goes.
lines.plain: The new project manager asked for twenty minutes on how a project goes. She does not need the documents. She has the documents; they are all in the archive. She wants to know how it goes.

lines.text: Somebody asks for something. You write down the ask, then the case for doing it at all, then the charter that says what it actually is, and somebody senior lets you plan. That is the first gate.
lines.plain: Someone asks for something. You write down the request. Then you write the case for doing it at all. Then you write the charter, which says what the project really is. Then a senior person allows you to plan. That is the first gate.
ref: RfP (Ready for Planning): at the end of the Initiating Phase

lines.text: Then you plan it properly, and discover that the four plans everyone forgets are approved by four different people and none of them by you. That is the second gate.
lines.plain: Then you plan it properly. You discover that the four plans everyone forgets are approved by four different people, and that none of them is approved by you. That is the second gate.

lines.text: Then you build it for two years, and every month you do the same small things. Report. Changes. Risks. Issues. Quality. Acceptance. Transition. The business side. Until the thing is in operation and the users have it in their hands. That is the third gate, and it is the last one.
lines.plain: Then you build it for two years. Every month you do the same small things: reporting, changes, risks, issues, quality, acceptance, transition, and the business side. You continue until the system is live and the users have it. That is the third gate, and it is the last one.

lines.text: Then you stop. You sit in a hot room and say out loud what you would do differently, you write it down for people you will never meet, you give everything to the archive, and the Project Owner signs. There is no fourth gate. Nobody comes and tells you that you were right.
lines.plain: Then you stop. You sit in a hot room and say aloud what you would do differently. You write it down for people you will never meet. You give everything to the archive. Then the Project Owner signs. There is no fourth gate. Nobody comes and tells you that you were right.
ref: The Closing Phase starts with the Project-End Review Meeting and ends with the Project Owner's (PO) final approval, which marks the project's administrative closure.

lines.text: And the benefits?
lines.plain: And what about the benefits?

lines.text: About a year later, in somebody else's report, on a floor you no longer work on. That is not the sad part. That is the shape of the thing.
lines.plain: They arrive about a year later, in someone else's report, on a floor where you no longer work. That is not the sad part. That is simply the shape of a project.

lines.text: If the three of you have finished. Florence asked me in July whether it works. I said January.
lines.plain: If the three of you have finished talking. In July Florence Nightingale asked me whether the system works. I said she should ask me in January.

lines.text: It works.
lines.plain: It works.

lines.text: And the honest version, which nobody asked for. The reconciliation is right every morning, including the two mornings I was certain it would not be. And two of my colleagues do a smaller job than they did in 2027, and one of them minds very much. Both of those are true, and only one of them will ever be in a report.
lines.plain: And here is the honest version, which nobody asked for. The reconciliation is correct every morning, including the two mornings when I was sure it would not be. And two of my colleagues now do a smaller job than they did in 2027, and one of them is very unhappy about it. Both things are true. Only one of them will ever appear in a report.

lines.text: Now come here. There is something you have never actually watched.
lines.plain: Now come here. There is something that you have never actually watched.

lines.text: On her screen, a disbursement to a programme country. Value date Monday. She types it once. The treasury system already has it, the payment gateway already has it, and she is done before the coffee arrives. Forty seconds, and nobody in this building will ever count them again.
